beats.headline: Is your microservice architecture a distributed monolith?
beats.subline: If you deploy services together, you're paying the complexity tax without the scaling reward.
beats.narration: If a routine feature change in Service A forces a deployment of Service B and C, you aren't doing microservices. You've built a distributed monolith—all the network latency of a distributed system with the tight coupling of a legacy codebase.

beats.title: Architecture Trade-offs

top.label: Modular Monolith

bottom.label: Microservices

beats.narration: A modular monolith keeps boundaries enforced by the compiler. Microservices move those boundaries across network hops. The distributed monolith is the worst of both worlds: separate deployments that still share a database and call each other in lockstep.

beats.title: The Microservice Reality
beats.subtitle: Decoupling at the storage and logic layer
beats.narration: True microservices own their data. If Service A writes to Service B's database, you have hidden schema coupling. Use async events to communicate, keeping each service's persistence isolated and protected.

beats.title: Database-per-Service Config
beats.code:
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://orders-db:5432/orders_db
    username: ${ORDERS_DB_USER}

# billing-service/application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://billing-db:5432/billing_db
    username: ${BILLING_DB_USER}

steps.explanation: Dedicated credentials and physical schemas prevent cross-service table access.
Billing cannot see Orders tables, forcing API-based communication.

beats.narration: Never share a database. Even if they sit on the same physical server, use separate schemas and credentials. This prevents noisy-neighbor contention and hidden coupling where one team breaks another's SQL queries.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Domain-Driven Design & Bounded Contexts →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we dive into Domain-Driven Design to stop slicing services by database tables and start slicing by business capability.

beats.headline: Why your 'Customer' class is a ticking time bomb.
beats.subline: Modeling one universal entity for every context is the fastest way to kill productivity.
beats.narration: If your Customer class has 60 columns used by shipping, billing, and marketing, you've created a monolith in disguise. Every change risks breaking unrelated workflows.

beats.title: Bounded Context Models

steps.explanation: Only cares about loyalty tier for order validation.
Only cares about tax and credit limits for invoicing.

beats.narration: Split the domain. The Ordering service doesn't need a tax ID, and Billing doesn't care about loyalty tiers. By defining context-specific records, you stop the ripple effect of changes across your entire system.

beats.title: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)

steps.explanation: Isolates legacy schema quirks from your clean domain logic.
If the legacy system changes, you only update this mapper.

beats.narration: When dealing with legacy systems, use an Anti-Corruption Layer. It maps ugly external data into your clean domain types. Your core business logic remains pristine, even if the legacy CRM changes its schema tomorrow.

beats.title: Strategic DDD
beats.subtitle: Defining boundaries by language
beats.narration: A Bounded Context is where your terminology has one consistent meaning. Use a shared UUID to link them, but keep the internal models completely separate. This is how you scale teams without constant coordination.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Solving Data Joins & Read Models →
beats.narration: Boundaries are set. In Part 3, we solve the biggest microservice headache: how to query data across services without breaking the database-per-service rule.

beats.headline: How do you join data when the tables are in different databases?
beats.subline: You can't use SQL joins anymore. Here are the two industry-standard patterns.
beats.narration: Once you split your databases, SQL joins are gone. You have two choices: API composition for simple lookups, or event-driven read models for complex search and pagination.

beats.title: API Composition (BFF)

steps.explanation: Fetches data from multiple services over HTTP/gRPC.
Combines them in memory for the frontend.

beats.narration: API composition is simple and returns fresh data. But it's chatty. If you need to filter or paginate across thousands of rows, this approach will fall over. That's when you need a replicated read model.

beats.title: Event-Driven Read Model

steps.explanation: Listens to events to build a local read-optimized table.
Uses version checks to handle out-of-order events.

beats.narration: For high-performance reads, project data into a local table. Use version numbers to ensure that older events don't overwrite newer state. It's eventually consistent, but lightning fast for complex queries.

beats.title: Query Patterns
beats.subtitle: Choosing the right strategy
beats.narration: Use API composition for simple ID lookups. Use event-driven read models for search, sorting, and pagination. Don't over-engineer simple screens with complex event projections.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): The 8 Fallacies of Distributed Systems →
beats.narration: Data is handled. In Part 4, we cover the eight fallacies of distributed computing—the assumptions that will crash your production system if you aren't careful.

beats.headline: Why your code works on your laptop but fails in the cloud.
beats.subline: The 8 fallacies of distributed computing are the silent killers of microservice reliability.
beats.narration: You can't assume the network is reliable, latency is zero, or bandwidth is infinite. These fallacies are why your local tests pass, but your production system flakes out under load.

beats.title: Local vs. Distributed
beats.narration: Local calls are reliable. Network calls are not. You need timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers. Never assume a request will succeed just because it worked in your dev environment.

beats.title: Distributed Survival
beats.subtitle: Defensive architecture
beats.narration: To survive, you need observability. Correlation IDs are non-negotiable for debugging requests across services. Without them, you're flying blind in a distributed environment.

beats.title: The Final Checklist
beats.caption: Before you split your monolith
beats.narration: Microservices are an organizational trade-off. If you aren't ready to handle the operational complexity, stay in a modular monolith. It's cheaper, faster, and safer.
